prompt: The designer hands you a new onboarding flow for a release in two weeks. It has custom animations between every step and a drag-and-drop photo editor. You estimate the full design needs about four weeks, while the core steps alone need about one and a half. What do you do first?
choices: Start building right away and work some extra hours, since a fast start may make the full design fit, and raise the gap only if you fall behind.
Show the designer and the product manager your estimate for each part, and propose releasing the core steps first, so that the date can still hold.
Tell the product manager the release has to move to four weeks, because cutting parts of the design would give new users a worse first experience.
Build the core steps and swap the animations and editor for simpler versions you choose yourself, so the date holds without a long discussion.
explanation: Best (3): "Share the estimate per part and propose a phased release". The people who own the design and the date get real numbers on day one, and the plan keeps the date while delivering the most important part. "Move the release to four weeks" (2): Honest and early, but it offers only one option and makes the trade-off for the product manager instead of with them. "Start and work extra hours" (1): Hides a known gap of about two weeks in the hope that it disappears; when it is raised late, there are fewer options left. "Simplify on your own" (0): Makes design and product decisions alone and hides them; the designer and product manager find out at release.

prompt: Three days before a new checkout launches, you test it with a screen reader and find that the payment step cannot be completed: the card fields have no labels and errors are never announced. A proper fix takes about two days. The launch date has been announced to customers. What do you do first?
choices: Launch on time and put the fix in the backlog for next sprint, since screen-reader users are a small share of customers and the date is public.
Fix it quietly over the next two days without telling anyone, so that the launch date is not put at risk by meetings and long discussions.
Since some customers cannot pay at all, tell your lead and the product manager now, show a short recording, and propose fixing it before launch.
Tell the product manager, and suggest launching on time with a note asking screen-reader users to order by phone until the next release.
explanation: Best (3): "Raise it now with evidence and propose the fix before launch". A whole group of customers cannot pay; the people who own the launch need to know today, and there is just enough time to fix it if the work is planned. "Launch and backlog it" (0): Knowingly ships a checkout that some customers cannot use at all; it excludes them and creates legal risk in many countries. "Fix it quietly" (1): The fix is right, but it uses most of the remaining time without telling the launch owners; if it slips, nobody has planned for it, and it gets no agreed testing time. "Suggest launching with a phone-ordering note" (1): Open with the product manager, but it proposes knowingly launching a payment step that a group of customers cannot use and gives them a separate, worse path, when the real fix fits before launch.

prompt: A sales manager asks for the new web app to also work in a six-year-old browser version, because one large prospective customer still uses it. Supporting it would need extra build tooling, make pages heavier for everyone, and add testing on old machines. The team has no written browser support policy. What is the best response?
choices: Agree to support it, since winning a large customer matters to the company, and add the old browser to the build and test setup this sprint.
Ask the sales manager how big the deal is and how many of the customer's staff use that browser, then send them a cost estimate so they can decide.
Add a few polyfills so the main pages mostly work in that browser, without full testing, so sales has something to show the customer soon.
Since the cost falls on every user, estimate it, then ask the product manager and sales to decide together and suggest writing down the result.
explanation: Best (3): "Estimate the cost and have the product manager and sales decide together". The cost falls on every user and on the team, so the person who owns priorities should decide with sales, using real numbers; suggesting that the outcome is written down stops the same debate from coming back with every deal. A Mid engineer brings the numbers and the right people together rather than making the call alone in either direction. "Get deal details and send sales an estimate to decide" (2): Good facts and a clear cost, but a decision that affects every user and the team's plans is left to sales alone, without the product manager. "Agree straight away" (1): Commits the team to a lasting cost for all users on the strength of one prospect, without anyone weighing it. "Quick polyfills without testing" (0): Creates a support promise the team cannot keep; the customer finds the broken parts after buying.

prompt: You are reviewing a teammate's pull request that adds a date picker to the settings page. The build report shows that the main JavaScript bundle, which every page loads, grew from 180 KB to 420 KB, because the picker brings in a large date library with all its languages. Everything works in testing. What do you do?
choices: Request changes with the bundle numbers, since every page pays the cost, and suggest lazy-loading the picker or a lighter library.
Approve it, since it works and the settings page needs a picker, and open a separate ticket to look at the bundle size some time later.
Ask the teammate to drop the library and use the browser's built-in date input instead, because the main bundle must not grow at all.
Approve it, then propose a build check that fails pull requests growing the bundle by over 10%, so tools catch this next time.
explanation: Best (3): "Request changes with numbers and options". Every page gets slower for a feature used on one page; the review is the cheapest moment to fix it, and the teammate gets facts and choices rather than a verdict. "Approve and ticket it for later" (1): Ships a large slowdown to every visitor; "later" tickets for performance are rarely done. "Insist on the built-in input" (2): Protects the bundle and may be a fine solution, but it dictates one answer, ignores whether it meets the design, and "must not grow at all" is not a real rule. "Approve and propose a budget check" (1): A budget check is a good idea for the future, but this pull request still more than doubles the bundle.

prompt: The designer wants the new sign-up form split into three short steps. The product manager wants one long page, because it is quicker to build. Each of them has asked you, separately, to start building their version this week. What do you do?
choices: Build the designer's version, since the designer owns the user experience and the extra build time is only about two days.
Build the product manager's version, since the product manager owns the priorities and the one-page form is quicker to deliver.
Bring them together, share what each version costs to build, and ask them to agree on one, so that you build it only once.
Start on the parts both versions need, such as validation and the API calls, and let them settle the layout between themselves.
explanation: Best (3): "Bring them together with the costs". The conflict is between two people who each own part of the decision; making it visible, with facts, lets them decide once, and nobody is surprised later. "Build the designer's version" (1) and "Build the product manager's version" (1): Each quietly picks a side, so the other person finds out later and the work may be redone. "Build the shared parts and wait" (2): Uses the time well and avoids taking sides, but leaves the conflict unresolved and the layout blocked.

prompt: Marketing asks you to add a third-party chat widget to every page by pasting the vendor's script tag into the page head. In a quick test, it adds about 1.5 seconds to page load on a mid-range phone and loads scripts from several other domains. Marketing wants it live by Friday. What is the best response?
choices: Add it as asked by Friday, since marketing owns this tool and its budget, and the vendor is a well-known company that many sites use.
Decline to add it, because third-party scripts slow the site down and are a security risk, and ask marketing to choose a different tool.
Add it by Friday with the async attribute so it blocks less, and check the page speed again next month to see whether customers complain.
Since every visitor pays the cost, share it with marketing and propose loading the chat later, only where needed, after a security review.
explanation: Best (3): "Share the cost, propose a lighter way to load it, review it first". Marketing gets its widget, users keep a fast site, and a script that runs on every page and talks to other domains gets the security and privacy check it needs. "Add it as asked" (1): Slows every page by 1.5 seconds and adds unknown third-party code with no review, without telling the requester about the cost. "Decline it" (1): The concerns are real, but refusing ends the conversation instead of solving marketing's need; choosing tools is not the engineer's call alone. "Add it with async and check later" (2): async is a real improvement and the date is met, but the script still loads on every page, nobody reviews it, and waiting for complaints is not a measure.

prompt: Your site shows a cookie banner, and the site's privacy notice says analytics only run after a visitor clicks "Accept". The marketing lead says too few people accept, and asks you to load analytics for every visitor as soon as the page opens, and to stop only if someone clicks "Reject". What do you do?
choices: Make the change as asked: marketing owns the analytics and the privacy notice, and knows best what the business needs from the data.
Explain that this would track people before they agree, against the notice, and ask the privacy owner to decide; offer other ideas.
Refuse in the chat thread, tell the marketing lead that the request is illegal, and say that you will report it if they ask again.
Build it behind a setting that is switched off, so it is ready to go if legal agrees later, and tell the marketing lead that it is done.
explanation: Best (3): "Explain the conflict and involve the privacy owner". The request breaks the site's own promise to visitors; the engineer explains why, sends the decision to the person responsible for privacy, and still tries to help with the real goal. "Make the change" (0): Knowingly tracks visitors against what the site tells them; marketing does not decide alone what the privacy notice allows. "Refuse and threaten to report" (1): The concern is right, but the tone and threat damage the relationship, and the engineer may not know what is legal where the site operates; it does not involve the privacy owner. "Build it switched off and say it is done" (1): Builds a feature that should not exist and gives a misleading status; one config change away from tracking without consent.

prompt: Support forwards a message from a customer who cannot use a mouse. On the "Book appointment" page, they can move around with the Tab key, but cannot open the date picker or reach the "Confirm" button. Your team built that page last month. What do you do first?
choices: Since your team built the page, try it with only the keyboard, note what fails, then fix it or raise a ticket with steps; keep support updated.
Ask support to suggest booking by phone, since the page works for most customers and the booking flow is not planned for changes this quarter.
Add tabindex="0" to every element on the page, so that everything can be reached with the Tab key, and then close the support ticket.
Log a low-priority ticket in the accessibility backlog, because only one customer has reported the problem so far and the team is busy.
explanation: Best (3): "Reproduce with the keyboard, then fix or ticket it, and update support". Confirms the real problem quickly, owns the team's page, and keeps the customer informed. "Suggest booking by phone" (0): Treats a broken page as the customer's problem and decides to leave the barrier in place for the quarter; many users who cannot use a mouse never report it, so one report usually means many affected users. It scores lower than the "use another browser for now" workaround in other items because it rules out a fix. "Add tabindex to everything" (1): A guess that does not make custom controls work with Enter or Space and creates a confusing Tab order; closing the ticket without testing hides that the problem remains. "Low-priority backlog ticket" (1): Records it, but rates a blocked booking as minor and leaves the customer with no answer.

prompt: Your company's privacy policy says that people get marketing emails only if they choose to. The product manager asks you to make the "Send me marketing emails" box on the sign-up form ticked by default, and to make its text smaller and light grey, so that more people end up subscribed. What is the best response?
choices: Make the change as asked, since the product manager owns sign-up numbers and people can still untick the box or unsubscribe later.
Make the box ticked by default as asked, but keep its text at the normal size and colour, as a fair compromise between both concerns.
Ask the legal team whether it is allowed and build whatever they approve, since that decision belongs to them and not to engineers.
Explain that this breaks the privacy policy and is meant to be missed, and find honest ways to grow sign-ups with the privacy owner.
explanation: Best (3): "Raise the conflict, offer honest options, involve the privacy owner". The request breaks the company's own promise that people choose marketing emails, and the small grey text is meant to make them miss the box. The engineer says so clearly, helps with the real goal, and brings in the person responsible for privacy. The key does not depend on any one country's law, because the company's own policy is what is being broken. "Make the change" (0): Builds a pattern meant to subscribe people without their choice, against the policy, with trust and legal risk. "Pre-ticked but readable" (1): Still subscribes people who did not choose to, so the main conflict with the policy remains. "Ask legal and build what they approve" (2): Brings in a right person, but the engineer does not point out the conflict with the policy themselves and offers no alternative that meets the product goal.

prompt: Two days before launch, the designer reviews the staging site and files 25 small tickets: spacing that is a few pixels off, a slightly wrong grey, an icon 2 px too low. You also have two real bugs to fix. After the bugs, you have time for about 10 of the small tickets. What do you do?
choices: Fix the two bugs first, then agree with the designer which ten matter most to users, so the rest are planned, not dropped.
Work through the designer's tickets in the order they were filed, since each one is quick and the designer is the expert on visual quality.
Fix the two bugs, then tell the designer the visual tickets will go into the next release, since there is not enough time for polish now.
Work late on both days to fix all 25 tickets and both bugs, so that the launch matches the approved design exactly as planned.
explanation: Best (3): "Bugs first, then agree the top ten with the designer". Real bugs come first, the limited time goes to the visual fixes the designer and you agree matter most, and nothing is silently dropped. "Tickets in filing order" (1): Leaves the real bugs for last and spends time on whatever was filed first, not on what matters most. "Bugs, then defer all visual tickets" (2): Right priority for the bugs, but some visual issues may matter (for example contrast or a misleading icon), and the designer is told instead of asked. "Work late to do everything" (1): Unlikely to fit, rushes changes into the last two days before launch, and hides the real capacity problem.

prompt: Your team's browser end-to-end test suite fails about one run in four, and people have stopped trusting it. A teammate proposes turning on automatic retries (up to three tries per test) so the pipeline goes green. In the failures you have looked at, tests wait a fixed two seconds instead of waiting for the page to be ready. What is the best response?
choices: Agree to turn on retries, since the testing tool supports them well, and go back to feature work, which is what the team is measured on.
Agree to retries if tests passing only on a retry are reported as flaky, and propose replacing the fixed waits too, since they are the cause.
Suggest removing the end-to-end suite and relying on unit tests, because a suite that nobody trusts gives the team no real value.
Reject retries, which hide real bugs, and offer to spend next week replacing the fixed waits in every test of the suite yourself.
explanation: Best (3): "Retries with flaky tests reported, and fix the cause". Retries unblock the team today, reporting tests that pass only on a retry keeps flakiness visible instead of hidden (most browser test tools can do this), and replacing fixed waits with waiting for the page to be ready removes the real cause, starting with the tests that fail most. "Turn on retries and move on" (1): The pipeline turns green, but flakiness is hidden, and real intermittent bugs will also pass on the second try. "Remove the suite" (0): Throws away the only tests that check the real user flows in a browser; unit tests do not replace them. "Reject retries and rewrite every wait yourself" (2): Goes after the root cause, and the worry about hidden bugs is fair, but the team keeps a suite that fails one run in four while one person rewrites everything, and reporting retried tests already answers that worry.

prompt: Your redesigned product page is behind a feature flag and is shown to 10% of visitors. After three days, 2.4% of the visitors who see it make a purchase, compared with 2.5% on the old page. The error logs show nothing unusual. The product manager plans to switch it on for everyone on Monday. What do you suggest?
choices: Go to 100% on Monday as planned, since the design was tested with users before launch, and a difference this small could easily be random noise.
Switch the redesign off for everyone until the design team can explain the drop, because lost sales cost the company more than any delay.
Since nobody has checked the drop yet, share the numbers with the product manager, hold at 10%, and find out whether it is real and why.
Raise it to 50% to collect data faster, and tell the product manager after the weekend, once the numbers are clearer and easier to read.
explanation: Best (3): "Nobody has checked the drop: share it, hold at 10%, find out why". The drop is small (2.5% to 2.4%) and may be noise after three days, but nobody has checked it. Holding at 10% is exactly what the flag is for: the team learns whether the drop is real and why (a slow page on some phones, a broken flow on one browser) while limiting the risk to 10% of visitors. "Go to 100% as planned" (1): The drop may be random, but nobody has checked, and the rollout would expose every visitor to a possible loss. "Switch it off for everyone" (2): Cautious and protects sales, and would be right for a large drop; for a small, unconfirmed one it stops the data that could explain it and hands the problem to another team. "Raise to 50% and tell the product manager later" (0): Increases exposure to a page that may lose sales, without telling the person who owns the rollout.

prompt: Three days before release, the translations arrive. In two languages, button labels and menu items are much longer than in English: text spills out of buttons, and the menu wraps onto two lines on small screens. What do you do?
choices: Ask the translators to find shorter words for the long labels, since the layout was designed and approved using the English text only.
Give buttons a fixed width and cut long labels off with "...", so that every button keeps exactly the size and shape shown in the design.
Suggest to the product manager that those two languages ship one release later, so that the layout can be fixed properly and tested first.
Make the layout cope with longer text (wrapping, flexible widths), so it works in every language, and test the longest ones on phones.
explanation: Best (3): "Make the layout handle longer text and test it". Translated text is often 30% or more longer than English, so the layout is what needs fixing; testing the longest languages on small screens confirms it. "Ask for shorter translations" (1): Puts the whole problem on the translators; shorter words often do not exist, and the next language will break the layout again. "Fixed width with ..." (1): Users of those languages cannot read what the buttons do. "Ship those languages one release later" (2): A reasonable fallback that protects quality, but it delays users of those languages when the fix is usually small.

prompt: You are building the screens for a new "order history" feature. The backend team says its API will be ready in about two weeks, but the response format is not final yet. Your part is due in three weeks. What is the best approach?
choices: Wait for the API before building the screens, since building against a response format that may still change would waste your work.
Agree a draft response format with the backend team, build against a mock of it, and test with the real API as parts become ready.
Choose the response format yourself, build the screens with mock data, and ask the backend team to match your format when they build it.
Build the screens with mock data shaped like the closest existing API, and adapt them when the real response format is ready.
explanation: Best (3): "Agree a draft contract, mock it, test early". Both teams work in parallel against the same agreed shape, and testing against real parts early finds differences while they are still cheap to fix. "Wait for the API" (1): Leaves one week for all the screens and any surprises in the API. "Choose the format yourself" (1): Productive, but it decides another team's API without them and invites conflict and rework. "Mock the closest existing API" (2): Keeps you moving, but the guessed shape may differ a lot, and nobody talks to the backend team until the end.

prompt: A customer reports that on their phone the "Pay" button is hidden behind the browser's bottom toolbar, so they cannot pay. You cannot reproduce it on the phones and simulators you have. Support has sent the customer's phone model, browser version and a screenshot. What do you do first?
choices: Close the report as "cannot reproduce": the page works on every phone and simulator that the team has tested it on so far.
Ask support to tell the customer to pay from a different browser or a computer, until more customers report the same problem with it.
Use those details to reproduce it on a matching device or a remote device service, and check how the page height is worked out there.
Add extra empty space at the bottom of every page on phones, which should push the Pay button above the browser toolbar for this customer.
explanation: Best (3): "Reproduce on a matching device and check the height calculation". The report has exactly the details needed; remote device services cover phones the team does not own, and full-height layouts (for example 100vh) often behave differently with browser toolbars. "Close as cannot reproduce" (0): Ignores a customer who cannot pay and the details they provided. "Tell the customer to use another browser" (1): A temporary workaround for one person, but nobody looks for the cause and other users quietly give up. "Extra space everywhere" (1): A guess that changes every page for all users without confirming the cause.

prompt: You are adding analytics to the new checkout. Another team already sends an event called "purchase_complete", but theirs fires when the payment form is submitted, while yours should fire only when the payment is confirmed. The marketing dashboard already uses their event. What do you do?
choices: Use a different name, such as "payment_confirmed", tell the other team and the analytics owner, and propose a shared list of event names.
Also send your event as "purchase_complete", since your meaning is the correct one for that name, and let the dashboard count both.
Use a different name, such as "payment_confirmed", and describe it in your team's own notes, since the other team's event is not your task.
Ask the other team to rename their event to match what it really means, and hold back your tracking until they have done it.
explanation: Best (3): "Different name, tell the others, propose a shared list". Keeps both meanings separate, warns the people who rely on the data that "purchase_complete" counts submissions rather than confirmed payments, and prevents the next clash. "Reuse the same name" (0): Mixes two different events under one name, so the dashboard silently double-counts and nobody can trust it. "Different name, documented only in your notes" (2): Your data is clean, but the misleading event and the risk of future clashes are left for others to discover. "Ask them to rename and wait" (1): Renaming would break the dashboard that already uses the event, and your tracking is blocked meanwhile.

prompt: To save time, a teammate suggests calling a paid maps service directly from the browser, with the service's secret API key in the frontend code. That key can also change and delete data in the company's maps account. The service offers restricted keys meant for browsers. What is the best response?
choices: Agree, but load the key from an environment variable at build time, so that the key never appears in the source code repository at all.
Agree, since the frontend code is minified before release and only logged-in users can open the page that uses the maps service.
Insist that all maps calls, including just showing the map, go through your backend, so that no maps key is ever sent to the browser.
Explain that anything sent to the browser is public, so propose a restricted browser key for showing maps and the backend for changes.
explanation: Best (3): "Browser code is public: restricted key for display, backend for changes". Anyone can read keys in frontend code; a restricted browser key (limited to your domain and to read-only use) is what the service offers for this, and actions that change data stay on the server. "Build-time environment variable" (1): Keeps it out of the repository, but the build puts the key into the JavaScript sent to every visitor, where it is still easy to read. "Minified and behind login" (0): Minifying does not hide strings, and any logged-in user (or anyone who creates an account) can copy the key and change company data. "Everything through the backend" (2): Secure, but it adds cost and latency for displaying maps when the service provides safe browser keys.

prompt: Early on a weekend morning, the site shows a blank page to most visitors. You find the cause: the app waits for an A/B testing script from an outside vendor before it renders, and the vendor's servers are down. The script can be switched off with a config change that is quick to deploy. You are on call. What do you do first?
choices: Switch the script off with the config change, check that pages render again, and post in the incident channel what you did and why.
Contact the vendor's support and wait for their fix, to avoid spoiling the A/B tests that are running now by switching the script off.
Change the app so it no longer waits for the script before rendering, and deploy that change, because it removes this risk for good.
Call the product manager who owns the A/B tests, ask whether you may switch the script off, and act as soon as they reply to you.
explanation: Best (3): "Switch it off, confirm, and tell the channel". The site is down for most visitors and there is a quick, safe, reversible fix; the on-call engineer uses it, checks that it worked, and keeps everyone informed. "Wait for the vendor" (0): Keeps the whole site down to protect experiment data, with no idea how long the vendor will take. "Change the app so it does not wait" (2): The cause is known and this is the right long-term fix (unlike a guessed quick fix), but writing, reviewing and deploying code during an outage is slower and riskier than flipping the existing switch; do it after. "Ask the product manager first" (1): Telling them is good, but you are the on-call engineer and the product manager does not own the outage; waiting for their permission at the weekend keeps the site down when the on-call engineer is trusted to take this kind of reversible action.

prompt: Your feature needs a button with an icon and a loading spinner. The shared design-system Button has no such variant. The design-system team cannot build one for about three weeks, but they accept contributions and usually review them within two days. Your feature is due in one week. What do you do?
choices: Copy the shared Button into your feature folder and add the icon and spinner there, since your team owns this feature and its date.
Agree the approach with the design-system team, then add the variant to the shared Button yourself and use it in your feature.
Wait for the design-system team's version, and tell the product manager the feature will be about two weeks late because of it.
Build a small separate button for your feature now, and add a ticket to replace it with the shared one once the variant exists.
explanation: Best (3): "Agree with the design-system team and contribute the variant". The team accepts contributions and reviews them in about two days, so the feature can ship on time with the shared Button, the library gains a variant everyone can use, and the owners agree the design. "Copy the Button" (1): A private copy that will drift from the shared one with every library update, with no plan to remove it. "Wait three weeks" (1): Delays the feature by two weeks for something you could help build. "Separate button with a replacement ticket" (2): Meets the date and plans a clean-up, but it creates a one-off component when the shared one could be extended in the same time, and replacement tickets often stay in the backlog.

prompt: In a pull request, a teammate renders article text from the company's content management system (CMS) with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. When you comment, they reply that only staff can edit the CMS, so the HTML is safe. You know that about 40 people, including freelance writers, have CMS accounts. What is the best response?
choices: Approve it, since your teammate knows the CMS better than you do, and it is true that customers cannot edit or create the articles.
Block the pull request until the CMS is changed to return plain text only, so that no HTML from the articles reaches the page.
Explain that one misused or hacked CMS account could put script on every article page, and suggest sanitising the HTML first.
Approve it, and open a ticket asking the security team to review the CMS and who has accounts on it when they next have time.
explanation: Best (3): "Explain the real risk and suggest sanitising". Forty accounts, some outside the company, are a real attack surface; sanitising with an allow-list (for example DOMPurify) keeps the formatting articles need and removes scripts. The reply gives a concrete reason and a cheap fix. "Approve because the teammate knows best" (0): Approves code you believe is unsafe, on a reason you know is not true; deferring to a teammate does not change the risk. "Block until the CMS returns plain text" (2): Removes the risk, but also removes the formatting the articles need and makes the work wait on a change in another system; sanitising does the same job without either cost. "Approve and ticket the security team" (1): Records the risk, but still ships a known script-injection path when the fix is small; a ticket does not protect readers in the meantime.
